title: A Year After Genesis Launch, AI ‘Dominating’ Scientific Advances, DOE’s Gil Says - HPCwire
html:
It’s been exactly a year and a day since President Trump unveiled the Genesis Mission, an ambitious Department of Energy plan to accelerate science and engineering through AI. The investment is paying off, as the impact of AI is being felt widely in science, the DOE’s Under Secretary for Science Darío Gil said during a panel at SC26 last week.

“There’s a lot of evidence that this is delivering results,” said Gil, the former head of IBM Research who was tapped to lead Genesis Mission in the fall of 2025, during a panel discussion at SC26 in Chicago last week. “If you just see the rate of progress of what’s happening in the last year across many fields and the impact that this has having with the scientists themselves….it is undoubtedly the force that is dominating not just the headlines, but the practical reality of how scientific advancements” are being made.

It would be tough to argue with Gil, especially on the math side of the equation, as we’ve seen several major AI breakthroughs in the field of mathematics in just the past two months. First, a researcher at OpenAI in September claimed that he had solved the Navier-Stokes problem using the Codex AI model. Then last week, a mathematician from Anthropic claimed to have used the Claude AI model to prove the Riemann hypothesis.

While we’re not seeing those types of headline-grabbing breakthroughs in science, we are seeing real progress being made. But more importantly, we’re seeing fundamental changes taking place in scientific workflows. The advent of agentic AI, in particular, is giving scientists and engineers powerful tools for offloading more monotonous aspects of science and engineering, as well as providing a source of idea creation.

“I think it’s hard for people to appreciate how much has changed in the last year-and-a-half or two years, that almost everything people are doing now–whether it’s coding or running on big machines or analyzing data from runs–is all being done with agents,” Rick Stevens, Argonne’s associate laboratory director for Computing, Environment and Life Sciences (CELS), told HPCwire in a recent interview.

AI is impacting scientific fields–including biology, drug discovery, physics, materials, and others–in multiple ways. First, it’s changing how scientists review literature and identify problems to tackle. It also is helping with setting hypothesis and experiment setup, as well as executing experiments and collecting data. AI is helping to analyze data and present findings as well.

These are all areas that the Department of Energy would like to accelerate with Genesis Mission, which was launched by an Executive Order on November 24, 2025. Led by Gil, the broad goal of Gensis is to double the productivity of the nation’s science and engineering productivity within 10 years, within three broad areas, including advancing research in energy, building new tools for AI-powered scientific discovery, and developing advanced AI technologies to ensure national security.

The Federal Government made a down payment on Genesis with $320 million in funding for the American Science and Security Platform (ASSP) in December 2025. That laid the groundwork for core Genesis components, such as the American Science Cloud (AmSC), the compute backbone of Gensis led by Oak Ridge National Lab, as well as the Transformational AI Models Consortium (ModCon), the software side of Gensis which is being led by Argonne National Lab along with the Pacific Northwest National Lab.

Genesis Mission Director Darío Gil at the Genesis Mission Summit in July

The ambitious plan originally looped in the 17 national labs plus an array of universities and IT vendors. It’s since been expanded to many others trough the Genesis Mission Consortium, as well as foreign partners like Japan via RIKEN. During the inaugural Genesis Mission Summit in July, the DOE announced 278 Phase 1 awards worth $179 million, as well as billions of dollars in additional funding of AI for science projects through other federal agencies, including NIH, NASA, and NSF, which has its own NAIRR project.

During the SC26 plenary panel last week, which was titled “The Ground Truth: AI’s Real Impact on Science and HPC,” Satoshi Matsuoka, the director of the RIKEN Center for Computational Science, said that his “ah ha” moment with AI for science occurred when he asked ChatGPT to replicate some of the award-winning COVID research that RIKEN did on the Fugaku supercomputer during the pandemic, which involved modeling the spread of the virus among the Japanese population.

“It was just prior to the time that the paper came out and we hadn’t published anywhere the results,” Matsuoka said. “I decided to see whether ChatGPT was smart enough to replicate the research. This was three or four years ago, and lo and behold …it identified the problems, it replicated the methods.

“That one just totally blew me away,” Matsuoka told the audience. “We have an AI scientist. Finally, the human being created an intelligence that can do science.”

The value of AI in science and engineering has been shown, and early adopters are moving quickly and getting good results. The challenge now is scaling the resources to the global community of researchers, and more importantly, sharing the knowledge of how to do science with AI.

“One of the animating philosophies that we have is that this is not something that is going to be done to the community, but rather, this is something that is going to be done with the community,” Gil said during the SC26 panel. “Now, what that means in practice is we’ve got to equip them with the tools and knowledge and the support, such that they can understand how to apply the incredible scientific instruments that are these AI supercomputers and quantum systems to come along with, obviously, decades of progress in HPC.”
summary: It’s been exactly a year and a day since President Trump unveiled the Genesis Mission, an ambitious Department of Energy plan to accelerate science and engineering through AI.
